lesson.title: Max und der kranke Montag
lesson.subtitle: Max pretends to be sick — his mother's thermometer has other ideas

hook.title: Before You Read
hook.content: A short, funny capstone story: Max wants a day off, so he invents an illness. Read for the plan, the evidence, and the moment the plan fails. One sentence uses the would-form (wärst / würdest); it is glossed, so you can enjoy the joke without stopping to build it.

footnotes.title: blass, Thermometer, Temperatur
footnotes.content: blass = pale; das Thermometer = thermometer; die Temperatur = temperature. These are the story's evidence words.

footnotes.title: Erkältung & Bauch
footnotes.content: die Erkältung = a cold (illness); der Bauch = belly. Mein Bauch tut weh = my belly hurts.

footnotes.title: wärst / würdest
footnotes.content: Wenn du wirklich krank wärst, würdest du nicht so schnell sprechen = If you were really sick, you would not speak so quickly. This is the would-world (Konjunktiv II); recognise the shape, do not produce it yet.

footnotes.title: seufzen & scheitern
footnotes.content: seufzen = to sigh; scheitern = to fail. Max seufzt. Sein Plan ist gescheitert = Max sighs. His plan has failed.

footnotes.title: Plan & Zimmer
footnotes.content: der Plan = plan; das Zimmer = room. Max's plan, and the room his mother enters.

pattern.title: Die Geschichte
pattern.content:
Es ist Montagmorgen. Max will nicht zur Schule gehen. Er liegt im Bett und hat eine Idee: Er sagt, er ist krank.

„Mama, mir geht es nicht gut!“, ruft er. Seine Mutter kommt ins Zimmer. „Du siehst blass aus. Hast du Fieber?“

Max sagt: „Ja, ich habe Fieber. Und mein Bauch tut weh.“ Seine Mutter holt das Thermometer. Max wartet und lächelt. Er denkt: „Mein Plan funktioniert.“

Die Mutter kommt zurück und schaut auf das Thermometer. „Max, du hast kein Fieber. Deine Temperatur ist normal.“ Max ist überrascht. „Vielleicht ist es nur eine kleine Erkältung“, sagt er. Die Mutter schüttelt den Kopf. „Wenn du wirklich krank wärst, würdest du nicht so schnell sprechen. Du gehst heute zur Schule.“

Max seufzt. Sein Plan ist gescheitert. Aber er denkt schon über einen neuen Plan nach.

exercises.prompt: Reading check — match each story sentence with its English meaning:

matching_pairs.english: Max does not want to go to school.
matching_pairs.german: Max will nicht zur Schule gehen.

matching_pairs.english: He says that he is sick.
matching_pairs.german: Er sagt, dass er krank ist.

matching_pairs.english: Max does not have a fever.
His mother sends him to school.
matching_pairs.german: Die Mutter schickt ihn zur Schule.

exercises.target_answer: Max will nicht zur Schule gehen., Er sagt, dass er krank ist., Seine Mutter holt das Thermometer., Max hat kein Fieber., Die Mutter schickt ihn zur Schule., Sein Plan ist gescheitert.
exercises.meaning: the story beats: the plan, the evidence, the failure
exercises.explanation: The six beats are a small courtroom scene: claim, evidence, verdict, consequence.

exercises.prompt: Why does Max stay in bed?
exercises.meaning: Max wants a day off, so he pretends to be sick.
exercises.explanation: The first paragraph says Max will nicht zur Schule gehen and then he says he is krank. The illness is the plan, not the cause.

exercises.prompt: How does the mother find out the truth?
exercises.meaning: The thermometer shows a normal temperature, so the mother knows Max is pretending.
exercises.explanation: The evidence is the thermometer: Du hast kein Fieber. Deine Temperatur ist normal. Max's speed of speech is the second clue.

exercises.prompt: What does the mother mean by 'Du bist nicht krank'?
options: She thinks he is very sick.
She wants him to stay home.
exercises.meaning: The mother sees through the act and sends him to school.
exercises.explanation: She has the thermometer evidence and says he speaks too quickly for a sick person. Her conclusion is that he is not ill.

exercises.prompt: Which English follows the German words most closely?
exercises.german: Er hat gesagt, dass er krank ist.
exercises.natural: He said that he is sick.
options: He has said that he sick is
He said that he is sick
He says that he was sick
He said that he is healthy
exercises.target_answer: He has said that he sick is
exercises.meaning: He said that he is sick.
exercises.explanation: The dass-clause sends the verb to the end: ... dass er krank ist = literally 'that he sick is'. English keeps 'that he is sick'; German keeps 'is' last.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — give the mother's verdict in German: 'He is not sick.'
twist.explanation: nicht comes after the verb: Er ist nicht krank. The mother's evidence is the missing fever; the verdict is this short sentence.

summary.outcome: Read a humorous Perfekt story, follow a claim-evidence-verdict structure, and read a dass-clause.

use_example.german: Er hat gesagt, dass er krank ist, aber seine Mutter hat kein Fieber gefunden.
use_example.english: He said that he is sick, but his mother found no fever.

summary.takeaway: A story can be a small argument: claim, evidence, verdict. The dass-clause puts the verdict's verb at the end, where the evidence lands.
summary.curiosity_teaser: You have finished the reading branches. Re-read any story for the pleasure of recognising the machinery.

fieber.context_translation: The child has a high fever.
fieber.etymology_derivation: Borrowed early from Latin febris — English fever shares the same Latin source via French. [wiktionary]

bauch.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *būkaz 'belly, body' — cognate with dialectal English bouk. [wiktionary]

krank.context_phrase: Ich bin krank und bleibe zu Hause.
krank.context_translation: I am sick and staying home.
krank.etymology_derivation: Old sense 'crooked, weak' — Wiktionary: cognate with English crank. [wiktionary]

mutter.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mōdēr — English mother and German Mutter are essentially unchanged siblings. [wiktionary]

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

montag.etymology_derivation: Moon-day: both name the day after the moon — English kept the moon's name, German kept the compound with Tag. [wiktionary]

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

bett.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *badją — explicitly cognate with English bed; the High German d→t gives the final -tt. [wiktionary]

zimmer.context_phrase: Mein Zimmer ist groß und hell.
zimmer.context_translation: My room is big and bright.
zimmer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *timrą — cognate with English timber: English keeps t, German shifted it to z. [wiktionary]

tag.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and y → g.

nacht.context_phrase: In der Nacht ist es hier sehr ruhig.
nacht.context_translation: At night it is very quiet here.

woche.context_phrase: Nächste Woche fahre ich nach Berlin.
woche.context_translation: Next week I travel to Berlin.

müde.context_phrase: Ich bin müde und gehe ins Bett.
müde.context_translation: I am tired and go to bed.
müde.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *mōþī; only Dutch moe named — no English cognate, memorize this one. [wiktionary]

falsch.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *falskī, from Latin falsus — the same Latin line as English false. [wiktionary]

arzt.context_translation: The doctor helps me a lot.
arzt.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German arzet, from Latin archīāter (chief healer); no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

vater.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fadēr; English f ↔ German v=[f] reflects Verner's-law voicing, not the v→b shift family. [wiktionary]

schule.context_phrase: Die Schule beginnt um acht Uhr.
schule.etymology_derivation: From Latin (ultimately Greek scholē) — the same classical loan as English school; see Schüler. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
